slides.title: Learning In High Dimensions
slides.notes: Open by naming the chapter problem as a pressure test for modern learning. Interpolation is easy for expressive models, but choosing the interpolant that behaves well away from the training set requires a bias. The lecture will move from ordinary smoothness to geometric structure, using the notebook figures as executable evidence.

slides.title: The Supervised Setup
slides.notes: Set up the formal language without dwelling on statistical learning theory. We have samples in a large ambient space, a target function, a parameterized class, and a risk measured on fresh points. The main danger is that matching every observed pair does not by itself say what happens between or beyond those pairs.

slides.title: Interpolation Does Not Choose
slides.notes: Use the figure as the first warning. Both displayed candidates pass through the training samples, so the training error check is nearly zero for each. Ask students to look between samples, where the functions disagree. That empty region is where generalization lives, and it is not controlled by interpolation alone.

slides.title: Regularity Selects A Winner
slides.notes: Move from existence to preference. A complexity score, such as a smoothness energy or norm, turns the interpolation constraint into a selection rule. The important message is not that splines solve all learning problems; it is that low-dimensional approximation works because regularity makes the unobserved regions less arbitrary.

slides.title: Bias Is A Restriction
slides.notes: Present inductive bias as a narrowing of possible functions, not as a vague taste for simpler answers. Universal approximation says many targets are representable, while the complexity map says which representatives the learner is willing to prefer. This distinction prepares the later shift from hand-written penalties to architecture-level priors.

slides.title: Optimization Can Add Bias
slides.notes: This slide is about implicit regularization. In an underdetermined linear system, there are infinitely many exact solutions, but gradient descent from the origin follows a path that lands at the minimum Euclidean norm solution. Treat this as a small, transparent model for a broader question: what preference does the training procedure secretly impose?

slides.title: Lipschitz Error Needs Fill Distance
slides.notes: Define the fill distance visually. If every new point is close to a training sample, a Lipschitz assumption transfers observed values to nearby unobserved values with a controlled error. The trouble is geometric: keeping the largest uncovered hole small becomes brutally expensive as the ambient dimension grows.

slides.title: Covering Growth Is Exponential
slides.notes: Read this as a sampling budget calculation. Halving a resolution scale in one dimension is manageable, but in dimension d the count is multiplied along every coordinate. The notebook ledger makes this concrete: a modest five cells per axis already gives more than thirty billion boxes in fifteen dimensions.

slides.title: Projection Priors Help Only When True
slides.notes: Use the projection artifact to separate a useful prior from a magical one. If the target depends on a few low-dimensional projections, a sparse or ridge-like model can reduce the apparent dimension. If the target uses long-range interactions across coordinates, the same prior can miss the signal while still looking beautifully simple.

slides.title: Geometry Replaces Ambient Smoothness
slides.notes: This is the pivot toward geometric deep learning. Instead of asking a function on raw Euclidean coordinates to be smooth everywhere, we ask which transformations of the domain are meaningful and how signals should respond. Locality, symmetry, and stability become sources of regularity that match the data-generating structure.

slides.title: A Blueprint For Taming Dimension
slides.notes: Turn the chapter into a design checklist. The learner should identify the domain, specify allowed transformations, choose equivariant or invariant layers, restrict information flow locally, and keep a diagnostic residual. This checklist is the bridge from the abstract curse of dimensionality to concrete architectures in the following chapters.

slides.title: Chapter Synthesis
slides.notes: Close by tracing the whole argument in one line. Rich models can interpolate; regularity chooses among interpolants; generic smoothness fails in high dimensions; special structure can reduce the effective search space. The exit question asks students to name the prior before naming the layer, which is the habit the rest of the course develops.
